chips.definition: A number printed in a NASA technical standard, cited with its requirement ID (or table).

A number from a NASA technical report that is not a standard and has no requirement ID: an OCHMO technical brief or an HRP evidence report. NASA-authored, cited in full. (The source kind keeps its original name, nasa_brief.)
A number from NOAA's operational Space Weather Scales; not a NASA crew-health limit.
A number from a peer-reviewed paper or another public document (for example a NASA fact sheet or presentation), cited in full.
Arithmetic on published values; the inputs and the formula are shown.
No published basis: LANDFALL's own number, labeled as ours, with the reason.

categories.name: Fitness for Duty
categories.glossary: Minimum measurable capability or capacity for a given physiological or behavioral parameter that allows successful performance of all required duties.

categories.name: Space Permissible Exposure Limit
categories.shape: ceiling on cumulative exposure over a time window
categories.glossary: Quantifiable limit of exposure to a spaceflight factor over a given length of time, e.g., lifetime radiation exposure.

categories.name: Permissible Outcome Limit
categories.shape: maximum change against the crewmember's own pre-mission value
categories.glossary: Acceptable maximum decrement or change in a physiological or behavioral parameter, during or after a spaceflight mission, as the result of exposure to the space environment. Biological/clinical parameter measured, e.g., bone mineral density.

categories.name: Operational scale (other agency)
categories.shape: level on a published operational scale (NOAA S-scale)

categories.name: Personal reliable change (Tier B)
categories.shape: reliable change against the crewmember's own recent baseline (single-case t-test, Crawford & Howell 1998)

categories.name: Countermeasure target
categories.shape: a published countermeasure target that is not a NASA limit (the renal case's 24-h urine output, from the HRP renal stone evidence report); capped at caution

tiers.definition: A fixed number NASA or NOAA publishes: a NASA standard (with its requirement ID, or a Table 4.8-1 row and column), a NASA report without a requirement ID (the renal TARGET rule, from the HRP evidence report), or the NOAA S-scale. The chip says which. One Tier A rule, ops_onboard_proton_s3, reuses NOAA's S3 number at Mars, where NOAA does not define its scale, so its chip is design choice.

Reliable change against the crewmember's own baseline: the single-case t-test of Crawford & Howell (1998), t = (value - baseline mean) / (baseline SD x sqrt(1 + 1/n)), df = n - 1, flagged when |t| exceeds the two-tailed critical value at alpha 0.001 (4.221 for a 14-day baseline). The idea of reliable change comes from Jacobson & Truax (1991); their arithmetic is not used.

severities.note: Exists in the type; LANDFALL never emits it. Emergency belongs to the vehicle caution and warning system.

source.rationale: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Appendix F gives the colour semantics (red reserved for Emergency/Warning); which LANDFALL finding maps to which class is ours.

rows.note: Countermeasure targets (NASA report) are not NASA limits, so never warning (rule field max_severity).
Personal change is not a limit, so never warning.
A non-alerting indicator (mood, daytime light, skin temperature) shows its reliable change but never alerts: advisory blue would read as an alert. Missing data still shows as advisory (row no_data).
[V2 10020]: indicate data that is stale, missing, unavailable, or unknown.
rows.colour_note: Severity advisory, but the colour is cyan, not advisory blue: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Appendix F Table F.5-1 requires cyan for 'Missing or stale data'.

principles.text: NASA publishes no numeric in-flight alert thresholds for crew health. Its alert requirements delegate the number to the program; LANDFALL never presents its own number as NASA's.
FFD (floor), PEL (ceiling on exposure over a window) and POL (maximum change from baseline) are never merged into one 'threshold exceeded' state.

refusals.text: No diagnosis. LANDFALL reports measurements against published limits and your own baseline; diagnosis is a flight surgeon's job.
No medication or dosing advice of any kind.
No psychiatric alert. Mood is private, never alerts, and leaves the device only with consent.
No personal cancer-risk (REID) model. NASA's 600 mSv career limit uses 35-year-old female model parameters for everyone ([V1 4030] note).
No claim that CO2 causes a cognitive deficit; the defensible claim is headache risk.
LANDFALL never raises an Emergency-class alarm; that belongs to the vehicle caution and warning system.
No radiation dose projection of our own; LANDFALL triggers on NOAA's scale or the onboard monitor.
No language model in the decision path; every rule is data you can read on /provenance.
